findings.description: FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/schema.toml` is internally incomplete relative to the advertised 4-layer facade because it defines no task-layer-only parameters at all. That makes the schema's layer model materially incomplete.

findings.description:
FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, `_compute_provenance()` contradicts its own docstring and returns incorrect provenance even when all files are valid. The docstring says it “records when each dotpath first appears or changes value,” but the implementation blindly assigns provenance for every dotpath present in each overlay file. Evidence: in the domain and task branches it does `for dp, val in _flatten_dict(domain_config).items(): provenance[dp] = ...` before/without checking whether `val` differs from the current merged value; in the model branch it does the same and also never merges into `current`. Therefore a lower layer that repeats an inherited value is still reported as the source layer, which is false under the stated “first appears or changes value” rule.
FOLLOW: This propagates directly into both public read APIs. `query()` exposes the wrong `PolicyResult.provenance`, and `get_parameter()` uses that map to populate `ParameterValue.source_layer`, so single-parameter lookups can lie about where a value came from. This also poisons any schema-validation pass that tries to reason from provenance, because repeated values look like effective overrides. The model-layer omission makes the error asymmetrical across layers, but the root cause is broader: provenance tracking is based on overlay presence, not on effective state transitions.

FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, `load_schema()` validates only three metadata fields (`type`, `constraint_class`, `min_layer`) and accepts malformed schema definitions for everything else, despite the module contract that every parameter has a defined type, default, constraint class, and minimum layer. Evidence from code: `default` is read with `defn.get("default")`, `description` with `defn.get("description", "")`, and `allowed_values` with `defn.get("allowed_values")`, with no shape/type/range checks at all. This means a parameter block missing `default` is accepted as `default=None`; an enum-like parameter can declare `allowed_values = "auto"` or `[1, 2]`; and a default can be outside the allowed set. Those malformed schema entries become first-class `ParameterDef` instances.
FOLLOW: This undermines every schema-based feature downstream. `get_parameter()` falls back to `defn.default`, so a missing or wrongly typed default becomes an effective runtime value. `list_parameters()` and `get_schema_for()` expose malformed metadata as if it were authoritative. Any later config-validation pass built on `allowed_values` can break or emit nonsense if the schema itself carries invalid `allowed_values`. This is a root-of-trust problem: if the schema loader is permissive, later validation cannot be trusted.
findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: validate `default`, `description`, and `allowed_values` inside `load_schema()` before constructing `ParameterDef`, rejecting malformed definitions.

findings.description:
FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, `validate()` performs only one-way coverage checks from registry hard-constraint sets to schema, but never checks the reverse direction: whether every schema parameter marked `constraint_class = "HARD"` is actually enforced by the underlying registry monotonicity machinery. Evidence: `validate()` computes `missing = registry_hard_* - schema_hard_*` for bool/threshold/string categories only. There is no corresponding `schema_hard_* - registry_hard_*` check. Therefore a schema author can mark a parameter as `HARD` and `validate()` still returns success even if that parameter is absent from `HARD_CONSTRAINTS`, `HARD_THRESHOLDS`, and `HARD_STRINGS`, meaning the registry will not enforce it.
FOLLOW: This creates silent false assurance about the advertised “15 HARD / 40 SOFT constraint classification.” The schema can claim a parameter is HARD, `list_parameters()` and `get_parameter()` will surface it as HARD, but lower layers may still weaken it because registry monotonicity does not know about it. This is architectural because the facade presents schema classification as authoritative while the actual enforcement lives elsewhere. It also compounds DSK001/ChatGPT_F001: even after adding per-file schema validation, monotonicity and schema can still diverge on what “HARD” means unless reverse coverage is checked.

FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, `diff_policies()` is not interface-compatible with the rest of the facade because it omits task comparison entirely and bypasses the facade’s own schema/default semantics. Evidence: signature is `diff_policies(domain_a, domain_b, model_a=None, model_b=None)` while `query()`/`get_parameter()` both accept `task_id`; then inside it calls `load_effective_policy(...)` directly instead of `self.query(...).effective`. As a result, the engine advertises a 4-layer hierarchy but its diff API can only compare 3 layers and returns sparse TOML differences rather than effective parameter differences under the facade contract.
FOLLOW: This means a user cannot diff two task-specific policies even though tasks are a first-class layer throughout the module and in the schema. It also means any future fix that normalizes `query().effective` with schema defaults will still leave `diff_policies()` semantically inconsistent unless it is routed through `query()`. This is a happy-path feature hole, not a corner case: task-level comparison is part of the stated system model.
findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: add `task_id_a` and `task_id_b` parameters and route the comparison through `query()` so diffing uses the same effective-policy semantics as the rest of the facade.

findings.description:
FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, method `diff_policies()`. The interface and semantic behavior are both incomplete. First, it omits `task_id_a` and `task_id_b` parameters, despite the underlying registry explicitly supporting a 4-layer merge (Layer 3 being task). This makes it impossible to compare task-level configuration overrides. Second, it compares the raw flattened TOML dicts (`flat_a` and `flat_b`) without resolving schema defaults. If `policy_a` falls back to the schema default of `0.5` implicitly, and `policy_b` explicitly states `0.5`, `diff_policies` flags this as a difference `(0.5, '<absent>')` despite their effective runtime behaviors being perfectly identical. 
FOLLOW: Users or validation harnesses attempting to verify configuration drift across tasks cannot use the API. For domains/models, any reliance on diffs will be polluted by false positives when default values are restated.
findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Expand the function signature to include `task_id_a` and `task_id_b`, and inject `self._schema` defaults during comparison to diff the true effective policies.

findings.description:
FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, function `_flatten_schema()`. The parser structurally forbids the word "type" from being used as a parameter name anywhere in the TOML configuration. Evidence: the heuristic `if isinstance(value, dict) and "type" in value:` attempts to distinguish leaf definitions from nested sections. If a schema author adds `[model.type]`, the `model` section dictionary will contain a key `"type"` (whose value is the parameter's definition table). The parser incorrectly triggers on the parent `model` section, attempting to parse the entire namespace as a single parameter definition.
FOLLOW: The parser immediately crashes with invalid configuration class errors for the section, and all other sibling parameters inside that section (e.g., `model.name`, `model.timeout`) are silently dropped from the schema.

FIND: `bench/cdsfl_registry/engine.py`, function `_compute_provenance()`. The method claims to record "when each dotpath first appears or changes value", but the merge simulation logic inside the method is entirely dead code. The variable `current` is maintained via `_deep_merge` for layers 1 through 3, but is never actually read to evaluate a value change. Consequently, provenance unconditionally stamps the highest layer that mentions a key, even for identical restatements. 
FOLLOW: `get_parameter().source_layer` reports false attribution for unchanged restatements. The dead `current` merge wastes CPU cycles and misled previous reviewers into thinking the merge process was meaningful but bugged (merging C0002).

FIND: `engine.py`, `PolicyEngine.query()` returns an incomplete effective policy. The method delegates to `load_effective_policy()` (which returns only merged TOML layers) but does not fill in default values for parameters absent in all layers. Evidence: lines 144–152 show `effective = load_effective_policy(...)` and `provenance = _compute_provenance(...)`, with no logic to inject schema defaults. The `PolicyResult.effective` dict will miss any parameter not explicitly set in universal/domain/task/model TOMLs, making it unusable as a complete policy.  
FOLLOW:  
1. `get_parameter()` correctly fills defaults (line 180: `if value is _MISSING: value = defn.default`), so single-parameter queries work.  
2. `diff_policies()` uses the same incomplete `load_effective_policy()` output, causing false differences when one policy has a default-filled parameter and the other doesn’t.  
3. Any caller relying on `query().effective` for a full policy will see missing keys, leading to `KeyError` or incorrect behavior.
findings.proposed_fix:
Modify `query()` to inject default values for all schema parameters missing from the merged TOML. Update provenance accordingly.
